item.title: Rethinking Sustainable Livelihoods From the Ground Up
item.dc:creator: Grita Anindarini
item.description: In regions where economic activity has long revolved around fossil-fuel extraction, ensuring a just transition requires developing alternative livelihoods that account for each community’s specific needs. Regional endowment funds could be a useful vehicle for funding these local initiatives.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Chaideer Mahyuddin/AFP via Getty Images

In regions where economic activity has long revolved around fossil-fuel extraction, ensuring a just transition requires developing alternative livelihoods that account for each community’s specific needs. Regional endowment funds could be a useful vehicle for funding these local initiatives.

By Grita Anindarini

JAKARTA—When the energy transition confronts difficult economic conditions within a country, addressing the transition’s unequal impact becomes both more challenging and more imperative. In Indonesia, with an economy recently described as a “ticking time bomb,” coal mining has long been the main driver of GDP in certain regencies and provinces. Pursuit of the energy transition in such places raises the tricky political question of how to support economic diversification, and boost economic growth, in these areas while also combating climate change.

The answer may seem obvious: reducing vulnerability to economic shocks caused by the shift away from fossil fuels requires broadening income sources. But that is easier said than done. A just energy transition requires a wider transformation that includes creating meaningful job opportunities, closing human-capital gaps, and alleviating poverty. Most importantly, these efforts must be highly localized to account for each area’s unique strengths and each community’s specific needs.

Pulau Panggung, a village located in Muara Enim, one of Indonesia’s most coal-dependent regencies, in South Sumatra province, illustrates this vulnerability starkly. According to research by WALHI Sumatera Selatan (Friends of the Earth South Sumatera) and the Indonesian Center for Environmental Law, 56.7% of the village’s residents are employed as mine workers, including casual laborers. When coal mining arrived in the early 1990s, the community largely abandoned farming, its main economic engine at the time. Now, as mining firms face expiring contracts and begin implementing efficiency measures, villagers’ livelihoods are under threat, but this time without a ready-made substitute.

The village’s post-coal economy could return to agriculture and embrace nature-based tourism. But shifting to these sectors requires a healthy ecosystem, making it essential to force companies to fulfill their obligations to restore mined land. Moreover, because villagers gave up farming decades ago, they would need training in sustainable agriculture techniques and opportunities to develop skills for other alternative livelihoods, such as digital-based marketing.

Some of the barriers to creating new livelihoods in Pulau Panggung are structural, such as the ambiguous legal status of land, a long-standing problem across Indonesia. But the bigger challenge, both here and elsewhere, is the lack of formal channels for developing effective local initiatives. Each village’s strengths must serve as the foundation for community-based economic transformation. Unfortunately, Indonesia’s top-down policymaking and regulatory regime, particularly in the energy sector, hinders efforts to maximize local strengths.

The Indonesian government directs transition planning by providing general guidance, which provincial and regency plans should theoretically elaborate on, identifying what is unique to each place. Yet the 2025–2029 South Sumatra medium-term regional development plan gives no clear direction on how economic transformation will be carried out, only that efforts to move away from a coal-based economy remain suboptimal. The plan recognizes that natural resources must play a role but does not explain how to use them in a way that fits the needs of each village and avoids harming ecosystems.

This problem is not unique to Indonesia. Many other governments have similar gaps in their energy-transition policies. The key is for policymakers to enable a more bottom-up approach by focusing on two objectives.

First, policymakers must directly involve affected communities. Entrusting transition planning to local governments and giving communities a genuine role in the decision-making process would help officials and companies design tailored interventions that expand employment opportunities for workers at risk of displacement.

Embedding community-driven initiatives in these policies must begin with local assessments. Before any plan is approved, the government should conduct participatory mapping of livelihoods, land status, workforce skills, and local strengths. In Pulau Panggung, this kind of mapping would highlight its agricultural and tourism potential.

Second, policymakers should explore the possibility of a regional fund that could redirect government revenue derived from mining and fossil-fuel production toward supporting community-based transitions. One model to follow is the Alaska Permanent Fund, whereby the state government invests a portion of its oil and mining revenues for the long-term benefit of all current and future Alaskans.

Managed by a state-owned corporation, this sovereign wealth fund helps finance public services like education, health care, and basic infrastructure. Policymakers, in both developed and developing countries alike, can use such a vehicle to ensure a sustainable economic transition by operating transparently and allowing local communities to direct the proceeds toward their chosen priorities.

Time is running out to establish regional endowment funds. Policymakers in Indonesia and other countries must act before mining and fossil-fuel revenues stop flowing. As a first step, they can run pilots in affected regions—like Muara Enim—to show what is possible. Waiting too long risks leaving these communities with a plan but no capital to implement it.

Grita Anindarini is a senior strategist at the Indonesian Center for Environmental Law.

Originally published on Project Syndicate

item.title: The Specter of an AI-Driven Slowdown
item.dc:creator: Dambisa Moyo
item.description: The rush to finance AI infrastructure is driving up borrowing costs just as governments grapple with mounting debt and persistent fiscal deficits. If the AI investment boom falters, falling valuations could choke off financing, with little room for fiscal and monetary policy to cushion the economic shock.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Myung J. Chun/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images

The rush to finance AI infrastructure is driving up borrowing costs just as governments grapple with mounting debt and persistent fiscal deficits. If the AI investment boom falters, falling valuations could choke off financing, with little room for fiscal and monetary policy to cushion the economic shock.

By Dambisa Moyo

ISTANBUL—Today’s economic growth depends heavily on AI investment and fiscal spending. The International Monetary Fund estimates that AI could add up to half a percentage point to annual global growth over the next decade, raising the average rate from 3% to 3.5%.

item.title: Is a Chinese Implosion Looming?
item.dc:creator: Navneeraj Sharma and Arvind Subramanian
item.description: If current trends continue, the Chinese state will find itself exposed to a political succession crisis, a weakening economy, and a lack of resources to exercise power domestically and project it externally. It would be a perfect storm, with far-reaching global repercussions.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Simon Song/South China Morning Post via Getty Images

If current trends continue, the Chinese state will find itself exposed to a political succession crisis, a weakening economy, and a lack of resources to exercise power domestically and project it externally. It would be a perfect storm, with far-reaching global repercussions.

By Navneeraj Sharma and Arvind Subramanian

NEW DELHI—This has been an era of shocks. In the space of two decades, the world has witnessed globally disruptive wars—from Iraq in the 2000s to Ukraine and Iran today—a global financial crisis, a global pandemic, and a rogue American president upending the global order. Now, yet another potential shock must be addressed: Though few dare to speculate about it publicly, an economic and political perfect storm is bearing down on China.

Continues on Project Syndicate (registration required)

item.title: PS Events: Reinventing Europe – Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala
item.dc:creator: PS editors
item.description: When we talk about "reinvention" we often overlook what works, noted WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala in her closing keynote. This is true of the global trading system, which has proven surprisingly resilient in recent years, and of the European economy, which might not have a tech giant to rival those in the US or China, but remains a global trade powerhouse and a leader in science and research. While Europe has much to do to improve its external competitiveness, it must not act from a sense of panic. Instead, it must pursue measured reforms and seize new opportunities, not least closer trade and investment ties with Africa.

item.title: Who Pays the Fiscal Watchdogs?
item.dc:creator: Janet Zhou
item.description: Civil-society oversight is the cheapest insurance in sovereign finance, because it enables independent scrutiny long before a default. But given that a borrowing government will never volunteer to fund the people who audit it, global decision-makers must do so using agreements for stolen-asset recovery and sovereign-debt treatments.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: z_wei/Getty Images

Civil-society oversight is the cheapest insurance in sovereign finance, because it enables independent scrutiny long before a default. But given that a borrowing government will never volunteer to fund the people who audit it, global decision-makers must do so using agreements for stolen-asset recovery and sovereign-debt treatments.

By Janet Zhou

HARARE—In 2021, Zimbabwean Finance Minister Mthuli Ncube caused an uproar when he issued more than $15 million in guarantees for private loans made by the Commercial Bank of Zimbabwe without seeking parliament’s approval. It was a particularly flagrant example of an unfortunately common practice in Zimbabwe: committing state resources to non-essential projects that offer no public benefit. Some of these loans invariably went unpaid, leaving taxpayers to cover the losses.

In April 2022, the Zimbabwe Coalition on Debt and Development (which I led at the time), together with three co-applicants, petitioned the High Court of Zimbabwe to declare that parliament must approve public borrowing before it happens. In March 2023, the Court ordered the government to gazette a bill in the next 12 months outlining parliament’s role in approving loans and guarantees and establishing the procedure for ratification or rejection.

This win was possible only because of a grant. The Open Society Initiative for Southern Africa, a regional foundation, funded the external lawyers who argued it, as well as our researchers, on a three-year cycle. When the cycle ended, the capacity to fight these legal battles went with it.

This model of financing public accountability in developing countries through grants has started to collapse. Aid from OECD donors fell by 23.1% in real terms in 2025, the largest annual drop ever recorded. Meanwhile, governments are tightening the requirements for registering civil-society organizations and limiting which of these groups can receive funding from abroad. Zimbabwe’s Private Voluntary Organisations Amendment Act, enacted in April 2025, allows the authorities to cancel the registration of civil-society organizations and seize their assets without judicial oversight. El Salvador’s Foreign Agents Law, passed just one month later, imposed a 30% tax on all foreign funding.

The weakening of civil-society participation will be felt widely, not least because every proposal for making global finance more sustainable and equitable depends on citizens who can read a debt-sustainability analysis and force a minister to answer for it. The Sevilla Commitment, adopted at last year’s Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, calls for strengthening parliamentary oversight of debt, independent audit institutions, and civil society’s role in exposing illicit financial flows. But nobody has said who pays for that work.

The answer may lie in two types of international instruments: agreements for stolen-asset recovery and sovereign-debt treatments. Each could contain a clause mandating that a fixed share of the sum—5% is a justifiable starting point—goes toward funding independent oversight of public finance in the recipient country. The money would be protected from executive interference, publicly audited, and guaranteed for the life of the program.

This has already been done in agreements for asset returns. In December 2017, Switzerland repatriated roughly $321 million stolen by former Nigerian President Sani Abacha under an agreement that provided for World Bank monitoring and civil-society oversight of how the money was spent. That same year, the United Kingdom, the United States, and four focus countries—Nigeria, Sri Lanka, Tunisia, and Ukraine—adopted the GFAR (Global Forum on Asset Recovery) principles, which commit governments that are returning or receiving assets to transparency and accountability.

But, to date, such monitoring has been treated as a courtesy, extended at the discretion of the government that happens to be holding the stolen funds. The Sevilla Commitment calls for piloting new approaches to asset return, including a clause in these agreements stipulating that a third party monitors the disbursement of money for oversight to prevent tampering from the recipient government.

Debt treatments, negotiated in creditor committees and multilateral fora, could adopt a similar approach: channel a fixed share of debt-service savings to an independently governed fund that supports public-finance oversight. Grants would be awarded competitively, published in a database, and externally audited against criteria written into the settlement.

Creditors have already accepted similar terms for different categories. In 1998, Uganda ring-fenced its debt-relief savings under the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries Initiative, earmarking them for anti-poverty programs. In 2023, Ecuador completed a debt-for-nature swap in which part of the interest on the new loan pays roughly $12 million annually, for 18.5 years, into a fund for maintaining the Galápagos Islands, governed by a board of representatives from government, academia, and business.

A borrowing government will never volunteer to fund the people who audit it. But when the obligation is written into these settlements, the money survives the next budget or election. It also gives creditors insight into the borrower’s disclosure practices.

Oversight is the cheapest insurance in sovereign finance. A group of economists tracking revelations of undisclosed debt across 154 countries over the past century found that nearly half of all sovereign defaults coincided with substantial upward revisions to reported public debt. Hidden debt piles up in good times and surfaces in bad times, when someone finally examines the books. If public oversight is properly funded, outside scrutiny begins long before a default and can pave the way for reform.

Consider the order that we won from Zimbabwe’s High Court. It was an important outcome that nonetheless failed to dent the problem. A bill was drafted but not gazetted; the Court’s deadline passed with no action. The organizations that could have fought in the courts for its enforcement had moved on to other grant-funded work.

As efforts to revamp the global financial architecture accelerate, policymakers must recognize that improving debt management starts with accountability at home. At the International Monetary Fund-World Bank Annual Meetings in October, the new Borrowers’ Platform, which seeks to give developing countries a stronger voice in global debt discussions, held its first Governing Council. While proactive coordination between finance ministers and central-bank governors, as the officials who sign the loans, is essential to achieve sustainable debt levels, it must be coupled with long-term external funding for civil-society groups that can hold them to their word.

Janet Zhou is Executive Director of the African Forum and Network on Debt and Development (AFRODAD).

Originally published on Project Syndicate

item.title: How to Help Left-Behind Regions
item.dc:creator: Keun Lee
item.description: Pouring public investment into poorer towns and cities might be politically beneficial, but the economic returns of indiscriminate largesse would be limited. A better approach would concentrate investment in areas with the potential to become high-productivity hubs, such as large peripheral cities.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Seung-il Ryu/NurPhoto via Getty Images

Pouring public investment into poorer towns and cities might be politically beneficial, but the economic returns of indiscriminate largesse would be limited. A better approach would concentrate investment in areas with the potential to become high-productivity hubs, such as large peripheral cities.

By Keun Lee

SEOUL—Discussion of economic inequality usually focuses on disparities across countries or the divide between rich and poor households within them. But greater attention is now being devoted to domestic regional differences, whether between the capital city and the rest of the country (as in South Korea and the United Kingdom), between northern and southern regions (as in Italy), or between coastal cities and inland areas (as in China and the United States).

item.title: The Agentic Information Economy
item.dc:creator: Shuwei Fang
item.description: An internet populated and run by AI agents will need not just reliable data but also a broader information ecology capable of questioning its own inputs and transmitting corrections where they are needed if information changes. But whether this will serve private interests or the public good remains to be seen.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Guillaume Souvant/AFP via Getty Images

An internet populated and run by AI agents will need not just reliable data but also a broader information ecology capable of questioning its own inputs and transmitting corrections where they are needed if information changes. But whether this will serve private interests or the public good remains to be seen.

By Shuwei Fang

CAMBRIDGE—Information is undergoing a category change. It has always been something people consume, but it is also becoming something machines act on. That means errors will stop being mere digital impressions and start becoming actions with far-reaching consequences. Given the risks, the system will need safeguards of its own. Better data or putting a human back in the loop will not suffice.

Continues on Project Syndicate (subscriber article)

item.content:encoded:
Photo: Dominika Zarzycka/NurPhoto via Getty Images

Extreme weather and climate-related events caused €822 billion in economic losses across the European Union between 1980 and 2024, with a quarter of the losses occurring just in the last five years. LUXEMBOURG—There is no choice between investing in resilience and investing in competitiveness. They are increasingly one and the same. Climate risk has become economic risk and a matter of economic security.

item.title: Nature Can’t Wait
item.dc:creator: Mary Robinson
item.description: Although the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine are spurring governments to increase spending on defense and focus more on economic growth, it would be a mistake to postpone investments designed to protect nature. In fact, meeting internationally agreed targets could add up to $450 billion to annual global GDP by 2050.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Luis Acosta/AFP via Getty Images

Although the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine are spurring governments to increase spending on defense and focus more on economic growth, it would be a mistake to postpone investments designed to protect nature. In fact, meeting internationally agreed targets could add up to $450 billion to annual global GDP by 2050.

By Mary Robinson

YEREVAN—In times of war, geopolitical turmoil, and fiscal tightening, it is tempting to view the defense of nature as a desirable but non-urgent goal—an objective that can be pursued when calmer times return. But we embrace this view at our peril.

As world leaders gather for the United Nations biodiversity and climate-change conferences this fall, they must remember that over half of global GDP depends on nature and the services it provides. Healthy soils underpin a $9.5 trillion global food industry, while forests support 1.5 billion livelihoods around the world. Healthy rivers help absorb floodwaters and sustain vital transportation networks. Nature is the backbone of the global economy, and protecting it must be a top national and international priority.

Nature-related crises won’t wait until the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine are over. This summer’s sweltering drought in Europe caused $2-3 billion in crop losses, a double blow for farmers after the war-induced closure of the Strait of Hormuz caused fertilizer prices to surge by 71%. The combined effects of conflict and extreme weather have helped push global food prices to their highest levels since 2022.

All told, scientists predict that a partial collapse of ecosystems could cost the global economy $2.7 trillion annually. Despite intense geopolitical instability, we cannot afford to undermine the natural systems on which our economies depend. The global goal to protect and conserve at least 30% of the world’s land and ocean by 2030, known as 30x30, is more important than ever.

Protecting nature is an investment in resilience and solidarity. Resilience strengthens food and water security, and the capacity to weather climate shocks. It sustains livelihoods, public health, and long-term economic stability. The 30x30 goal, adopted by governments in 2022 under the landmark Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, recognizes that protecting nature is fundamental to providing these and other public goods.

For example, kelp beds, mangroves, and marshes absorb carbon dioxide, while coral reefs help protect against storms and provide natural habitats for some of the world’s most diverse ecosystems. On land, forests regulate rainfall and support the livelihoods of local communities, and healthy soils retain water and nutrients that are vital to global food security and flood protection.

Four years on, the world has made significant strides toward the 30x30 goal. New analysis from Campaign for Nature shows that 20% of land and inland waters are now designated as protected or conserved, and that fully delivering on existing commitments could increase this share to approximately 27% by 2030, closing much of the remaining gap.

Progress at sea, however, has been much slower. Only 10% of the ocean is formally designated for conservation, and existing commitments would increase this to a mere 12% by 2030. Worse, Together for the Ocean’s latest Ocean Protection Gap Report finds that only 3.5% of the ocean is assessed as effectively protected, with harmful activities continuing in many areas that are supposed to be off limits.

With just four years remaining, the world still has a chance to achieve 30x30, which is one of the defining global commitments of this decade. But what will it take to make up for lost time?

For starters, governments must dramatically increase financing for nature. Delivering 30x30 will require approximately $100–180 billion annually, compared with current annual spending of $24 billion. But, again, this spending represents an investment, not just a cost. Achieving 30x30 could add up to $450 billion to annual global GDP by 2050 and support an estimated 4–7 million jobs.

Policymakers at all levels urgently must move from talking about solutions to implementing them. As of May 2026, 116 countries had submitted commitments to protect up to 27% of land and inland water areas. But many have yet to follow up with mapped, costed, and financed plans. Commitments alone will not protect nature.

Protecting more of the planet is only part of the challenge. Governments also must ensure that protected and conserved areas are well managed, deliver real benefits, and meaningfully preserve biodiversity. That requires long-term funding arrangements that can endure through changing economic and political cycles.

There is no denying that the global outlook is uncertain. The wars in the Middle East and Ukraine are spurring governments to increase spending on defense and focus more on economic growth. But it would be a mistake to put nature on the back burner. Protecting natural systems is not just for the bees. Investing in their future is an investment in our own.

Mary Robinson is a former president of Ireland and a former UN Secretary-General’s special envoy for climate change.

Originally published on Project Syndicate

item.title: Argentina’s Economic Chainsaw Massacre
item.dc:creator: Jeremy Adelman
item.description: Argentine President Javier Milei may currently be a lynchpin in US President Donald Trump’s geoeconomic vision for Latin America; but he could soon become its weak link. With elections coming next year, he has achieved an economic recovery and relative price stability by driving millions of his people into destitution.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Carol Smiljan/NurPhoto via Getty Images

Argentine President Javier Milei may currently be a lynchpin in US President Donald Trump’s geoeconomic vision for Latin America; but he could soon become its weak link. With elections coming next year, he has achieved an economic recovery and relative price stability by driving millions of his people into destitution.

By Jeremy Adelman

BUENOS AIRES—Nearly three years after Javier Milei became Argentina’s president, the chainsaw-wielding free-marketeer has established himself as the darling of the far right. Brazil’s right-wing presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, is promising an economic policy that would follow Milei’s lead, and US President Donald Trump calls him his “favorite president.” Last year, Trump extended Argentina an unprecedented $20 billion currency swap line to halt its currency’s free fall on the eve of legislative elections, and the gambit worked. Milei’s party won a surprising victory.

item.title: Which AI Myth Will We Embrace?
item.dc:creator: Richard K. Sherwin
item.description: The mythos—or foundational stories—that we tell ourselves will determine our fate in the age of AI. As industry leaders regale us with utopian visions of benevolent digital gods delivering scientific breakthroughs and expanding our technological horizons, our best defense against hubris is a counternarrative of social cooperation.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: DEA Picture Library/DeAgostini via Getty Images

The mythos—or foundational stories—that we tell ourselves will determine our fate in the age of AI. As industry leaders regale us with utopian visions of benevolent digital gods delivering scientific breakthroughs and expanding our technological horizons, our best defense against hubris is a counternarrative of social cooperation.

By Richard K. Sherwin

NEW YORK—It is telling that Anthropic chose to call its most powerful AI model “Mythos.” In ancient Greek, the word denotes an original reality that we can imitate or embody through the stories we tell ourselves and one another. Pliny the Elder tells us that the fifth-century Greek painter Zeuxis rendered grapes so realistically as to fool even the birds.

item.title: No More Superpowers
item.dc:creator: Carl Bildt
item.description: Although the United States remains very powerful and Russia still commands enormous conventional and nuclear capabilities, each country’s global status has come to be defined by failure and constraint. If anything, both may belong to the same broad grouping of middle powers that includes the likes of Canada, Brazil, and India.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images

Although the United States remains very powerful and Russia still commands enormous conventional and nuclear capabilities, each country’s global status has come to be defined by failure and constraint. If anything, both may belong to the same broad grouping of middle powers that includes the likes of Canada, Brazil, and India.

By Carl Bildt

STOCKHOLM—As the term “middle powers” has gained currency this year, it has forced us to ask which countries actually belong to this grouping. After all, shouldn’t most states be described that way?

item.title: What’s Driving Persistent Inflation?
item.dc:creator: Şebnem Kalemli-Özcan
item.description: In their preoccupation with high public debt, rising bond yields, and dizzying AI valuations, investors have seemingly forgotten the supply shocks shaping the underlying inflation outlook. But anyone worried about debt and yields must reckon with the disruptions created in the name of protecting domestic markets.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images

In their preoccupation with high public debt, rising bond yields, and dizzying AI valuations, investors have seemingly forgotten the supply shocks shaping the underlying inflation outlook. But anyone worried about debt and yields must reckon with the disruptions created in the name of protecting domestic markets.

By Şebnem Kalemli-Özcan

PROVIDENCE—It was only a few months ago that investors were preoccupied with US tariffs and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. But these issues have since receded from the forefront of our concerns, overshadowed by anxiety over the AI boom and possible bust, rising bond yields, and mounting public debt.

item.title: Building the Economy Africa Needs
item.dc:creator: Yemi Kale
item.description: Africa cannot control global geopolitics, let alone prevent external shocks. But it can manage its exposure, especially by building an integrated continental market, investing in higher-value-added production, and pushing for reform of the global credit-rating agencies.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Olympia de Miasmont/AFP via Getty Images

Africa cannot control global geopolitics, let alone prevent external shocks. But it can manage its exposure, especially by building an integrated continental market, investing in higher-value-added production, and pushing for reform of the global credit-rating agencies.

By Yemi Kale

ABUJA—As geopolitical tensions reshape the world economy, Africa faces a choice: it can allow itself to be carried along by events into an uncertain future, or it can use the ongoing shifts in the international order as an opening to position itself as a more influential global player.

item.title: Science Without Scientists?
item.dc:creator: Sami Mahroum
item.description: Now that autonomous systems are capable of generating their own hypotheses, designing experiments, and writing up the results, the scientific community must adapt. For scientific knowledge to retain its standing, its sources must be trusted and answerable to the public.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Joan Cros/NurPhoto via Getty Images

Now that autonomous systems are capable of generating their own hypotheses, designing experiments, and writing up the results, the scientific community must adapt. For scientific knowledge to retain its standing, its sources must be trusted and answerable to the public.

By Sami Mahroum

PARIS—Given current AI capabilities, does it matter who conducts scientific research? The intuitive response is that a fact is a fact, regardless of who finds it. But knowledge is never disseminated that way. We receive most scientific claims without any means of checking them ourselves, so we tend to judge not the claim but the credibility of whoever stands behind it. As the Harvard historian of science Steven Shapinshows, the production of scientific truth has long been inseparable from the social work of persuading one’s peers.

item.title: When Smart Cities Turn Menacing
item.dc:creator: Wairagala Wakabi
item.description: Uganda has embraced digital-surveillance tools in the name of improving public safety and combating terrorism, a pattern that is repeating itself across several African countries. But governments are increasingly using these technologies for political control, rather than for national security.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP via Getty Images

Uganda has embraced digital-surveillance tools in the name of improving public safety and combating terrorism, a pattern that is repeating itself across several African countries. But governments are increasingly using these technologies for political control, rather than for national security.

By Wairagala Wakabi

KAMPALA—In June 2025, Uganda switched on the Automated Express Penalty System (EPSAuto), using CCTV cameras, automatic number plate recognition (ANPR), and an intelligent transport monitoring system (ITMS) to fine motorists. But the system, ostensibly aimed at bringing order to the country’s chaotic roads, quickly generated controversy.

item.title: Brazil Cannot Afford Bolsonaro’s Spending Cuts
item.dc:creator: Laura Carvalho and Joseph E. Stiglitz
item.description: If he wins the October 25 runoff, far-right presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro plans to slash public spending by as much as 1.5% of GDP. These cuts could push Brazil into recession, hurt workers and small businesses, and drain tax revenue—all without solving the country’s debt problem.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Anderson Coelho/AFP via Getty Images

If he wins the October 25 runoff, far-right presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro plans to slash public spending by as much as 1.5% of GDP. These cuts could push Brazil into recession, hurt workers and small businesses, and drain tax revenue—all without solving the country’s debt problem.

By Laura Carvalho and Joseph E. Stiglitz

NEW YORK—Brazil faces a stark choice on October 25, when far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro and President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva face off in the country’s presidential runoff.

item.title: A Generational Reckoning on the Streets of Paris
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Levy
item.description: As their schools deteriorate and the planet grows hotter, many young people in France do not have hope for a decent future. The recent protests may foreshadow a broader conflict between older generations who wield political power and younger people who must live in the world they leave behind.

As their schools deteriorate and the planet grows hotter, many young people in France do not have hope for a decent future. The recent protests may foreshadow a broader conflict between older generations who wield political power and younger people who must live in the world they leave behind.

By Jonathan Levy

PARIS—After weeks of mounting tension on the streets of Paris, my wife and I decided to take our six-year-old daughter and leave town during Saturday’s protests. When the main demonstration assembled at 2 p.m. at the Place de la République, we were hiking in the forests southeast of Paris near Fontainebleau, once an autumnal retreat and hunting ground for French kings.

item.title: The Algorithm Driving French Student Protests
item.dc:creator: Gabriela Ramos
item.description: One of the main drivers of the student protests in France is the opposition to Parcoursup, the country’s university-admissions platform, which is widely denounced as opaque and unfair. While such automated decision-making systems do not create educational inequalities, they can exacerbate them.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Jeff Pachoud/AFP via Getty Images

One of the main drivers of the student protests in France is the opposition to Parcoursup, the country’s university-admissions platform, which is widely denounced as opaque and unfair. While such automated decision-making systems do not create educational inequalities, they can exacerbate them.

By Gabriela Ramos

PARIS—Hundreds of thousands of young people have taken to the streets in France to protest against the state of the country’s education system. The violence that erupted on October 17 should not eclipse their concerns, which are entirely legitimate: the deplorable conditions at many French schools, including dilapidated buildings, a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms, and long school days. They are also deeply opposed to Parcoursup, the country’s university-admissions platform, which has become the lightning rod for their grievances. They have denounced it as opaque, stressful, and unfair.
